speaker: Percy Liang
title: No Priors Ep. 7 | With Stanford Professor Dr. Percy Liang
question: In AI evaluation, why do traditional static, accuracy-focused benchmarks break down when assessing general-purpose language models?
guest: The trouble with evaluating language models is that a language model is a very generic thing—it's like saying "evaluate the Internet." It takes text in and text out, and can be used for a myriad of different applications. So we need to systematically lay out the scenarios where models are used and measure not just accuracy, which most benchmarks focus on, but also robustness, calibration—whether the model knows what it doesn't know—fairness, bias, toxicity, and efficiency. Another challenge is that new models keep coming out constantly, so evaluation has to update dynamically with new models and new scenarios. As capabilities increase, the things we ask of a language model change: we don't just ask it to do question answering or sentiment, we ask it to write emails, essays, or give advice, so benchmarks must add scenarios capturing those new capabilities and new risks like persuasiveness and security. One thing I'm especially worried about is jailbreaking: if these models start interacting with the world and accepting external inputs, you can not only jailbreak your own model, you can jailbreak other people's models and trigger a cascade of errors.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Static, accuracy-focused benchmarks were designed for narrow models with a single well-defined task, and several of their assumptions fail for general-purpose language models.

First, they saturate and leak. Fixed test sets get absorbed into training data, and models quickly hit ceiling scores, so results reflect memorisation or benchmark-specific tuning rather than real capability (Goodhart's law in action).

Second, a single accuracy number assumes one correct answer per input. General-purpose models produce open-ended output where many responses are valid, and quality depends on things accuracy ignores: reasoning, calibration, robustness, safety, fairness, helpfulness and efficiency.

Third, the task space is unbounded. No fixed dataset can cover everything these models are used for, so a benchmark score has weak construct validity: it measures performance on that dataset, not the underlying ability, and it poorly predicts behaviour in interactive, multi-turn, tool-using deployments.

Finally, results are fragile. Scores shift with prompt wording, formatting and sampling settings, which makes comparisons unreliable.

This is why the field is moving toward dynamic, multi-metric, human-in-the-loop and regularly refreshed evaluations.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
Traditional static, accuracy-focused benchmarks break down for general-purpose language models because fixed test sets cannot capture open-ended capabilities or withstand web-scale memorization. Because models train on massive internet corpora, public benchmarks frequently leak into pretraining or post-training data, causing data contamination that conflates genuine generalization with rote recall. Fixed datasets also suffer from rapid saturation and Goodhart’s law: models quickly hit performance ceilings while developers optimize specifically for leaderboard scores rather than broad competence. 

Furthermore, simple accuracy assumes a single, closed-form ground truth, such as a multiple-choice selection or exact string match. That framing fails to evaluate open-ended, multi-turn, and agentic interactions where quality depends on nuance, reasoning soundness, factual calibration, safety, cost, and alignment with diverse human preferences. Static evaluations are also notoriously brittle, as minor changes in prompt formatting can trigger wide accuracy swings without any change in underlying capability. Consequently, high static benchmark scores often lack ecological validity, failing to predict how reliably, safely, or usefully a model will perform across dynamic real-world contexts.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Static, accuracy-focused benchmarks were built for narrow systems. Each had one task, a fixed test set and a clear right answer. General-purpose language models break almost every one of those assumptions.

First, their capabilities are open-ended. A model can do thousands of tasks, so any fixed benchmark covers only a small part of what it does. Second, benchmarks get contaminated and saturated. Test items leak into web-scale training data, and models quickly approach ceiling scores. High numbers can then reflect memorization or overfitting to the benchmark rather than real ability. Third, many important outputs, such as essays, code, advice or dialogue, have no single correct answer. Exact-match accuracy misses quality, helpfulness and reasoning. Fourth, accuracy alone ignores things that matter in practice: calibration, robustness to rewording or adversarial inputs, fairness, toxicity, safety, efficiency and behavior over multi-turn or agentic use. Results are also sensitive to prompt wording, so scores can move a lot with small formatting changes. Finally, a static test can't keep up with fast-moving models or new risks.

This is why the field is moving toward holistic, multi-metric, dynamic and human- or model-judged evaluations, such as HELM, Chatbot Arena and red-teaming.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer:
Traditional static, accuracy-focused benchmarks break down for general-purpose language models because they were designed for narrow tasks with a single correct answer, whereas modern models operate across open-ended, interactive domains. First, static public datasets suffer from data contamination: because language models train on vast web corpora, test items often leak into training data, making it difficult to distinguish genuine reasoning from memorization. Even without leakage, frontier models rapidly saturate fixed benchmarks and exploit superficial shortcuts, turning scores into poor proxies for real-world capability.

Equally important, binary accuracy cannot capture what matters most in general-purpose use. Real-world tasks—such as drafting, coding, or multi-turn problem-solving—rarely have one ground-truth output; their quality depends on nuance, helpfulness, coherence, safety, and user intent. Static evaluations also miss how models behave under shifting prompts, novel contexts, and ongoing interaction, while ignoring vital operational properties like calibration, hallucination rates, and robustness. As a result, high benchmark accuracy increasingly diverges from practical reliability and usefulness.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Traditional benchmarks assume a fixed set of tasks, a known correct answer for each item, and an accuracy score that reflects how well the model will perform in practice. General-purpose language models face open-ended requests where several answers may be valid and quality depends on context, user intent, and how the answer will be used. A model can score highly while still fabricating facts, missing constraints, or failing when a prompt is rephrased. A single average can also hide rare but consequential failures.

Static test sets lose value over time. Their questions can leak into training data, developers can tune models to the test, and scores can approach the ceiling even while real-world performance varies widely. Accuracy remains useful for tasks with clear answers. Broader evaluation also needs fresh tasks, realistic interactions, and measures of qualities such as factuality, robustness, and instruction following.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Static benchmarks work best when the task is well defined, the test cases represent future use, and each answer can be scored reliably. General-purpose language models operate across tasks that users can reshape with a prompt or a follow-up. Many requests have several valid answers, and exact-match scoring can reject a good response or reward one that gets the final answer right through faulty reasoning.

A single accuracy score also hides differences that matter in practice. Two models can earn the same score while differing sharply in reliability under rephrasing, performance on rare cases, or ability to recognize uncertainty. Public test questions can enter training data, making it hard to distinguish memorization from generalization. Static scores still tell us how a model performed on a particular test, but they provide limited evidence about how it will behave in a new situation.
